newsitem.title: USA: Illinois district bond case back in court.
newsitem.headline: Illinois district bond case back in court.

text.p: A lawsuit challenging property taxes used to pay off debt issued by a suburban Chicago park district is headed back to court Tuesday.

The lawsuit was filed by a group of business owners in DuPage County who claimed the Lisle Park District's use of an aggregate extension of property taxes to pay off the debt violated a state of Illinois law limiting such taxes.

A DuPage County Circuit Court judge, who ruled in the plaintiffs' favor last April, will decide Tuesday whether he will reconsider his ruling at the request of lawyers representing the county collector.

Judge John Darrah ruled in April that the property taxes used by the park district to pay off general obligation debt issued for the retirement of approximately $6 million of installment contracts and alternate bonds were subject to limitations under a 1991 state tax cap law.

That law subjected park districts and other local governments in five suburban Chicago counties to an annual limit in property tax collection increases of five percent or the rate of inflation, whichever is less. Any increase in taxes over that limit require voter approval, under the law.
Darrah ruled that all taxes levied in excess of the limit were illegal and void and that the plaintiffs were entitled to a refund.

He rejected arguments that a 1983 amendment to the Illinois park district code allowed districts to issue general obligation debt to pay off installment contracts or to refund loans, and that existing obligations to issue GO debt would be immune from any subsequent change in state law.
If ultimately upheld, Darrah's ruling could have broader consequences beyond the Lisle Park District.

C. Richard Johnson, an attorney at Schiff Hardin & Waite, Lisle Park District's bond counsel, said Darrah's ruling would impact "virtually every park district" in DuPage County that pledged to issue GO bonds to retire installment contracts or alternate bonds. He said the ruling would force districts to use revenues from their operating property tax levies to pay off the debt.
Johnson said that would be "disasterous" for the districts, which need operating revenues to pay operating expenses to run parks.
Peter Murphy, general counsel of the Illinois Association of Park District's, said the group views the lawsuit "very seriously."
"It would have a tremendous negative impact on the ability of park districts to pay back bondholders, but to also deliver services," Murphy said.

Kim Paetschow, director of the Lisle Park District, said if Darrah's ruling is ultimately upheld the result would be "traumatic" for her district. She said the district would have to refund $384,000 for taxes it levied to pay debt service from 1991 to 1994.

Paetschow said the district's issuance of annual rollover GO debt to pay off debt incurred before the 1991 tax cap law took hold was done under the belief that such debt was grandfathered. She added that none of the debt was publicly sold, but was privately placed with banks.

Court filings for the motion for Judge Darrah to rehear the case claimed his ruling would unconstitutionally impair Lisle Park District's contract with holders of its installment contracts whether or not there is a default by impairing the district's pledge to issue GO debt to pay them off.
The filings also claim that GO debt sold to pay off alternate bonds was statutorily authorized and exempted from the tax cap law.

Attorneys at Chapman and Cutler, which served as bond counsel for some of the other park districts in the county, did not return phone calls. Attorneys at Chapman are also serving as special assistant state's attorneys in the lawsuit.
Susan Crowley, a Chicago attorney representing the plaintiffs, declined to comment on the case.
Paetschow said that an appeal to the Illinois Appellate Court will be filed if Darrah declines to rehear the case.
Also waiting in the wings is possible legislation to be introduced in the Illinois General Assembly to remedy the situation, she said.
--Karen Pierog, 312-408-8647
